title: Rāga Bhūpālī: Ascent and Descent
summary: A profile table for Bhūpālī (Kalyāṇ thāṭ, pentatonic, Ga–Dha as vādī–saṃvādī, first watch of the night, calm and grave) with its ascent, descent and pakaḍ. Śloka 148 sets the working order: split the scale by register into small groups, elaborate, add rhythm, carry it into tālas, then compose a song or gat.

blocks.verse:
विभागो लघुसंघातो विस्तारो लय योजला।
प्रवर्तनं हि तालेषु ततो गीतादिकल्पना।१४८।
blocks.text: Division [of the scale], small clusters [of notes], elaboration, setting [them] in laya (tempo), and carrying [them] through the tālas; after that comes the composing of songs and the like.

Once the theoretical introduction has been gained, then by the rule of nature, first divide the ascent and descent of the rāga into the three saptakas (registers) and make small pieces in those notes, whose size is governed by mātrās (beats). After that, on the basis of those same groups of notes, let the rāga be elaborated by the rule of nyāsa (resting notes) and so on. Then, from that elaboration of notes free of laya (tempo), plan tāns (fast runs) bound to laya in full measure. Then carry those tāns through various tālas with the help of tempos such as dogun (double). Then at last the conception of a song or gat can succeed.

Material things too are usually made in this same order. For example, bricks from clay, walls from bricks, and a building from walls. Wood from a tree, and a bed and so on from wood. Flour from wheat, and bread (roṭī) from flour.

Now, following the rules in the śloka written above, first divide rāga Bhūpālī into the three saptakas (registers) and show small ascents and descents as follows. (1) Sa Ḍha P̣a, P̣a Ḍha Sa. (2) Sa Re Ga Pa, PaGa Re Sa. (3) Pa Dha Ṡa, ṠaDhaPa. (4) Ṡa Ṙe Ġa Ṗa, Ṗa Ġa Ṙe Ṡa.

Now some svarasaṅghātas (clusters of notes) of four mātrās each are being made on the basis of these same notes. It is hoped that practitioners (sādhakas) will reflect on the order of the following clusters and on their features, and in the same way will themselves make clusters of different numbers of mātrās in various rāgas, practising them in writing and in playing, and will become so skilled that in every musical composition they will see nothing but clusters. Then they will try out their own understanding in other rāgas too.
